item.title: Dynamic correlation network and structure-aware matching for robust point cloud registration
item.description:
The problem

Point cloud registration finds the rotation and translation that align two partially overlapping 3D scans of the same scene, for example LiDAR or RGB-D scans captured from different viewpoints. Learned methods describe each point by features aggregated from its neighbourhood and then match points across the scans. When the relative rotation between the scans is large, these features, and the correlations between them, can change with the orientation, and the matches become unstable.

The common remedy is to train with randomly rotated scans, but augmentation cannot cover the continuous space of 3D rotations, SO(3), so orientations not seen in training still degrade performance. Rotation-equivariant networks such as PARE-Net help, yet they still combine neighbouring features through a fixed MLP that applies the same correlation model to every neighbourhood. And even when two superpoints are correctly matched, the individual points inside them can still be paired wrongly.

How it works

The method follows the coarse-to-fine pattern: a backbone extracts coarse superpoints and dense point features, superpoints are matched first, and points are then matched only inside matched superpoint patches. It changes two parts of this pipeline. A Dynamic Correlation Network (DCN) inside the PAREConv-FPN backbone decides how to combine neighbouring features from rotation-invariant cues, and a Structure-Aware Point Matching (SAPM) module refines the point matches inside each patch.

  1. Rotated input. The two scans arrive at an arbitrary relative rotation; the network has to estimate the rigid transform between them even when that orientation was not seen during training.
  2. A rotation-invariant cue. For each point and its nearest neighbours, a vector-neuron encoder builds features from the relative offsets, the mean offset of the neighbourhood and their cross product. These features rotate with the scan; their magnitudes do not, so the magnitudes serve as a rotation-invariant descriptor.
  3. Dynamic kernels. A channel reallocation network turns that descriptor into softmax scores over a small bank of learnable kernels (four in the experiments), and each neighbour’s kernel is the score-weighted sum of the bank. Because the scores depend only on invariant quantities, kernel selection does not change with rotation, while the aggregated features remain rotation-equivariant.
  4. Context inside each patch. Each matched superpoint pair defines two local patches. SAPM refines every point’s descriptor with linear self-attention over its own patch, at a cost linear in the patch size; points that lie closer to a different superpoint are masked out.
  5. Consistent matches and the pose. A row-wise and a column-wise masked softmax over the patch similarity matrix are fused with per-point confidence scores, and mutual top-k entries become dense matches. Each patch yields a pose hypothesis by SVD, and a feature-based hypothesis proposer keeps the best one, without RANSAC.

Results

Registration recall 95.4 % on 3DMatch and 79.6 % on 3DLoMatch; the 3DLoMatch result is the highest of all methods compared (Table 3).
Transformation recall 82.3 % on 3DLoMatch and 82.7 % on rotated 3DLoMatch, where FCGF drops by 15.1 points (Table 4).
Rotation error 0.21° on KITTI, the lowest of the compared methods, with 4.8 cm translation error and 99.8 % recall (Table 2).

3DMatch and 3DLoMatch are indoor benchmarks with overlaps above 30 % and between 10 % and 30 %; KITTI consists of outdoor driving scans. On 3DMatch the method is close to the best RANSAC-based method, BUFFER-X (95.6 %), and slightly ahead of DFAT and PARE-Net (both 94.9 %); with RANSAC in place of its own estimator it still reaches 95.2 % and 79.3 %. When arbitrary rotations are applied to 3DLoMatch, methods that rely mainly on rotation augmentation, such as FCGF and Predator, lose transformation recall, whereas methods with rotation-invariant or equivariant designs, this one included, stay stable. On KITTI, CAST has a lower translation error (2.5 cm), while this method has the lowest rotation error. In the KITTI ablation, DCN and SAPM each reduce the errors on their own, and together they lower the rotation error from 0.239° to 0.211° and the translation error from 5.5 cm to 4.8 cm (Table 6). The model has 4.04 M parameters and takes 100.29 ms on an RTX 4090, faster than CAST (129.80 ms) and PARE-Net (122.80 ms) (Table 5).

The authors note two limitations: when the overlap is critically small, coarse superpoint matches can be wrong, and highly repetitive structures can produce ambiguous descriptors that mislead hypothesis selection.

item.title: SuP: Sub-cloud Driven Point Cloud Registration
item.description:
The problem

Point cloud registration finds the rotation and translation that line up two 3D scans of the same scene. Modern methods do this precisely when the two scans share a lot of geometry. In applications such as large-scale mapping and autonomous navigation, though, the views often share only a small part of the scene. Once the shared surface falls below about 30 %, classic ICP and learned methods alike struggle to find reliable correspondences, and registration slows, drifts or fails.

The paper traces these failures to the regions that are not shared: they can still be geometrically or semantically similar to each other, and matching the two whole clouds then produces wrong correspondences that obscure the correct ones. Earlier work tried to predict which points lie in the overlap, but that prediction depends on consistent features and becomes less effective on low-overlap pairs. Later methods strengthen the features with attention, geometric encodings, semantics or colour, yet their accuracy still drops as overlap falls.

How it works

SuP changes what it looks for. Two scans may overlap only a little overall, but if each is cut into smaller pieces and the pieces are matched pairwise, a subset of these sub-cloud pairs has high overlap. SuP calls these high-overlap pairs anchor pairs. It finds them in two phases, then builds its matches only from inside them.

  1. Features for the whole scan. A KPConv backbone extracts point features at several scales, and attention layers exchange context within and between the two scans. By default SuP uses the colour-enhanced backbone and attention of ColorPCR.
  2. Subdivide. Each scan is split into k sub-clouds. Farthest point sampling picks well-spread centroids, and each sub-cloud collects a centroid’s nearest neighbours within a radius.
  3. Phase I: overlap-guided prior weighting (OPS). For every source–target pair of sub-clouds, SuP measures how strongly their point features agree, counting only mutual top matches, and keeps the best-scoring pairs as candidates. This is an efficient first filter against pairs that do not overlap.
  4. Phase II: multi-scale post-weighting (MPN). Each candidate pair is aligned with a preliminary pose from a weighted SVD. A small learned network then checks whether points that now sit close together also have similar features, at two scales. The pairs with the highest feature-consensus weights become anchor pairs. During training, the network is supervised by how well each candidate actually aligns (an alignment-aware weighting loss).
  5. Merge-to-match. Inlier correspondences from all anchor pairs are merged, refined on the denser points, and passed to a standard estimator (RANSAC or the RANSAC-free LGR) to compute the final rotation and translation.

In the reported setup, each scan is cut into 6 sub-clouds, giving 36 possible pairs. OPS keeps 24 of them, and the top 8 by feature consensus become anchor pairs.

Results

Registration recall 97.8 % on Color3DMatch and 90.2 % on Color3DLoMatch with the RANSAC-free LGR estimator, the highest among the methods compared with LGR (Table 2).
98.1 % and 90.4 % with RANSAC, and the highest registration recall at every sampling level from 5,000 down to 250 correspondences (Table 1).
Lowest pose errors: 1.374° / 0.046 m on Color3DMatch and 2.493° / 0.074 m on Color3DLoMatch (Table 3).

The evaluation uses colour-enhanced versions of the indoor 3DMatch benchmark: Color3DMatch, with pairs overlapping by more than 30 %, and Color3DLoMatch, the harder split with 10–30 % overlap. Registration recall is the share of scan pairs aligned to within 0.2 m RMSE. SuP uses ColorPCR’s colour-enhanced backbone by default; compared with ColorPCR alone, the strongest baseline, it raises recall from 96.5 % to 97.8 % on Color3DMatch and from 88.3 % to 90.2 % on Color3DLoMatch under LGR. The share of correct matches rises as well: with 250 sampled correspondences on Color3DLoMatch, 76.0 % of SuP’s matches are correct (inlier ratio), against 68.0 % for ColorPCR.

The sub-cloud step also works as an add-on to other methods. Added to GeoTransformer, it raises Color3DLoMatch recall from 74.0 % to 76.7 %; added to PEAL, from 81.2 % to 83.4 % (Table 4). In the ablation study, adding the four components one at a time (OPS, the feature-consensus weights, MPN and the alignment-aware loss) raises recall at every step on both benchmarks (Table 5). Sub-cloud size matters as well: smaller sub-clouds may lower recall because of insufficient overlap, larger ones miss local detail, and the default radius setting τ = 0.35 gives the best balance (Table 6). The paper’s limitation section notes that features from scans captured with very different sensors could weaken OPS and MPN, and suggests feature normalisation or domain adaptation as a next step.

item.title: DeSC: Learning Deep Semantic Descriptor for NeRF Registration
item.description:
The problem

A Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) stores a scene inside a neural network. Large scenes are often split into several NeRFs, and images captured without reliable global camera poses produce NeRFs that each live in their own coordinate frame. To combine them, one has to estimate the rigid rotation and translation between two independently trained NeRFs: NeRF registration.

Existing methods rely on either geometry or rendered colour. DReg-NeRF samples a point cloud from each NeRF and regresses correspondences, but these point clouds are noisy and contain artifacts from inaccurate density estimates, especially when a NeRF is under-trained. VF-NeRF optimises with a photometric loss, which makes it vulnerable to textureless and highly symmetric cases. Both ignore the view-independent embedding that a NeRF computes internally for every 3D point, which carries both geometry and appearance. Using it directly is not straightforward either: the two NeRFs are trained separately, so their embedding spaces do not match.

How it works

DeSC treats each NeRF as a source of point features, not only of geometry. It samples a point cloud from each NeRF, extracts geometric features with a KPConv backbone, and adds a Deep Semantic Aggregation Module (DSAM) that turns the NeRF’s own embeddings into descriptors that agree across the two NeRFs. A Transformer and a coarse-to-fine matcher then find correspondences, and the pose is solved by SVD.

  1. Sample each NeRF. DeSC takes the centres of the non-empty voxels in each NeRF’s occupancy grid and keeps those whose density exceeds a threshold σt. KP-FCNN downsamples this point cloud hierarchically and extracts multi-level geometric features.
  2. Query embeddings around each coarse point. For every coarse point, a patch is formed from its k nearest dense points within a radius τ. Each patch point queries the NeRF for its view-independent embedding, which is enriched with the point’s colour and density through a sinusoidal encoding, so that the features carry photometric information shared by both NeRFs.
  3. Aggregate with a texture-aware graph convolution. A graph convolution runs over each patch. Its edge weights emphasise points that are close to each other but have contrasting features, capturing local high-frequency texture. The output is fused with the geometric features to give the deep semantic descriptor.
  4. Add context and match. Geometric self-attention and cross-attention let each point cloud gather context from itself and from the other. Coarse correspondences are selected from the resulting features and refined on dense points with an optimal transport layer.
  5. Solve the pose. Outliers are removed, and SVD gives the rotation and translation that align the two NeRFs. During training, a density-aware photometric consistency loss also asks matched patches to have similar density-weighted colour.

Results

Registration recall 97.7 % on Objaverse, against 92.1 % for VF-NeRF and 94.5 % for SIRA-PCR, with a rotation error of 2.57° (Table I).
90.6 %, 91.0 % and 88.1 % registration recall at 30 % overlap on DTU, LLFF and Mip-NeRF360, against 86.6 %, 88.5 % and 84.8 % for VF-NeRF (Tables III–V).
Removing all proposed modules lowers Objaverse recall to 93.2 % and raises the rotation error to 9.19° (Table VI).

The object-level benchmark is built from Objaverse: for each object, 120 rendered images are split into two blocks, each block is given a random transformation, and a separate NeRF is trained on each; 44 objects unseen during training are used for testing. Registration recall counts the pairs whose estimated transformation has an RMSE below 0.2 m. DeSC is compared with the NeRF registration methods DReg-NeRF and VF-NeRF, and with eight point cloud registration methods run on points sampled from the NeRFs. With uniform noise of 10 % of the scene size added, its recall is still 95.74 % (Table II).

On the real-scene datasets DTU, LLFF and Mip-NeRF360, each scene is split into image subsets with 30 %, 50 % and 80 % overlap. DeSC has the highest registration recall in all nine settings, and the margin is largest at 30 % overlap, although VF-NeRF reaches a slightly lower rotation error in some settings. In the ablation, adding the deep semantic aggregation, the photometric encoding, the texture-aware edge weights and the photometric consistency loss in turn raises Objaverse recall step by step: 93.2 %, 93.9 %, 95.1 %, 96.9 % and 97.7 %.

The authors state two limitations. DeSC relies on NeRF’s implicit embeddings, so it does not apply directly to explicit representations such as 3D Gaussian Splatting, voxel grids or hash-based methods. Objects that are highly symmetric in both shape and texture, such as a traffic cone, yield symmetric features and can be matched wrongly, even when the rendered alignment looks plausible.

item.title: SemReg: Semantics-Constrained Point Cloud Registration
item.description:
The problem

Point cloud registration finds the rotation and translation that line up two partially overlapping 3D scans of the same scene, so that they can be merged into one. Recent learned methods describe every point by the shape around it, let the two scans exchange information through cross-attention, and then match points. Shape alone is often ambiguous, though: partial scans of a bed and a table can look geometrically alike. Cross-attention also lets every region of one scan interact with every region of the other, including pairs that are unlikely to overlap, such as a chair in one scan and a table in the other. These superfluous interactions lead to wrong matches.

Indoor scans captured with RGB-D cameras come with colour images, and semantic understanding is far more mature for 2D images than for 3D geometry. An earlier cross-modal method, PCR-CG, added image colour to the 3D features, but it uses only colour, not the semantic content of the images, and its features remain inconsistent.

How it works

SemReg is a 2D–3D cross-modal network. It keeps a standard 3D backbone for shape features and adds a semantic signal taken from the RGB frames, which it uses in three places: inside attention, at matching time, and in the training loss.

  1. Two scans with their colour frames. The input is a pair of partially overlapping point clouds, each with its RGB images. A KPConv backbone downsamples each cloud and extracts local shape features.
  2. Semantic features from the images. A pretrained DINOv2 network, kept frozen, extracts features from the RGB images. Using depth and the camera parameters, these are projected onto the 3D points and added to the shape features in self-attention.
  3. A semantic prior guides cross-attention. For each source point, SemReg finds the target points whose semantic features closely resemble its own and places a Gaussian over 3D distance around each one. The mixture of these Gaussians, the Gaussian Mixture Semantic Prior (GMSP), weights cross-attention so that features interact mainly between semantically similar regions.
  4. Matching within similar semantics. The Semantics Constrained Matching module sets the score of a candidate pair to zero when the semantic prior says the two points belong to unrelated regions. During training, a Semantics Aware Focal Loss supervises only pairs that are semantically related.
  5. Pose from the surviving matches. The final rotation and translation are estimated from the correspondences with RANSAC, and can be refined further with ICP.

Results

Registration recall 94.7 % on 3DMatch and 75.9 % on 3DLoMatch, the highest of all methods compared on both (Table 1).
95.4 % and 77.4 % after ICP refinement (Table 2).
Replacing all four semantic components with standard counterparts drops recall to 92.1 % and 66.5 % (Table 3).

The evaluation uses 3DMatch, an indoor RGB-D benchmark, and its low-overlap split 3DLoMatch (scan pairs with 10–30 % overlap). Registration recall is the share of scan pairs whose estimated transformation is accurate to within 0.2 m (RMSE). SemReg leads on both splits, ahead of SIRA-PCR on 3DMatch and GeoTransformer on 3DLoMatch, and in the paper’s ICP-refinement comparison its margin over the next-best method grows to 1.5 and 2.9 points. The semantic components matter most when overlap is small: they account for 9.4 points of recall on 3DLoMatch, against 2.6 points on 3DMatch. In one extreme case with 12.53 % overlap, where the only shared object is a chair, the semantic prior still locates the chair in the target scan and the registration succeeds, while GeoTransformer fails.

SemReg matches at a coarse level, with 0.1K–1K correspondences per pair against 6K–7K for dense methods such as GeoTransformer. Its inlier ratio is therefore lower than that of some competitors, although its registration recall is higher. Results on the outdoor KITTI dataset are reported in the supplementary material. The method needs RGB images aligned with the scan, so it does not apply directly to standalone point clouds; the authors suggest rendering images from the point cloud as a future workaround.

item.title: TopFormer: Topology-Aware Transformer for Point Cloud Registration
item.description:
The problem

Point cloud registration estimates the rotation and translation that align two partially overlapping scans. Most learned methods describe each point by its local geometry, match the descriptors, reject outliers with RANSAC and solve for the transformation. Recent Transformer-based methods work on a sparse, sub-sampled set of points and let every sparse point attend to all the others, and some add the points’ relative positions so that attention knows where each point sits.

Sub-sampling throws away fine-grained structure, though, and relative position does not help when two sparse points are close to each other in space but far apart along the surface. The paper’s example is the top of a chair next to the corner of a desk: the two points have similar local geometry because they lie in the same neighbourhood, and their relative position barely separates them because they are close in Cartesian space. Their features become ambiguous and lead to wrong matches. In the dense point cloud the difference is easy to see, since the route from one to the other along the surface is long; in the sparse points it is hard to observe.

How it works

TopFormer follows a coarse-to-fine registration pipeline and adds one ingredient: a topological structure encoding that tells the Transformer how each pair of sparse points is connected along the surface. Because the sparse points are a subset of the dense points, this surface information can be measured on the dense cloud and handed to the sparse points, which the authors call a sparse-through-dense strategy.

  1. Close in space, far along the surface. A KPConv encoder extracts local features at a sparse and a dense level. Two sparse points such as a chair top and a desk corner can look alike to it, and their relative position does little to separate them.
  2. Sparse points inside the dense graph. Down-sampling uses furthest point sampling, so every sparse point is also a dense point. On the dense points, TopFormer builds a K-nearest-neighbour graph, keeping only edges shorter than a radius τ.
  3. Geodesic distance by shortest path. For two sparse points p and q, Dijkstra’s algorithm on the dense graph gives the geodesic distance from p to q, the length of the shortest route along the surface.
  4. Direction from normals, independent of their sign. Normals estimated by PCA are unoriented, and scans can be in arbitrary poses, so the normals are hard to re-orient consistently. TopFormer therefore uses the sines of the angle between the normal at p and the vector from p to q, and of the angle between the two normals; flipping a normal turns an angle α into π − α and leaves the sine unchanged.
  5. Encoding inside attention, then matching. The geodesic distance, the Euclidean distance and the two sines are mapped by a sinusoidal function into the topological structure encoding, which is added to the keys of self-attention. Cross-attention then lets the two clouds exchange information; sparse points are matched from a confidence matrix, the matches are refined at the dense level with an optimal transport layer, and RANSAC estimates the final rotation and translation.

Results

Registration recall 92.4 % on 3DMatch and 75.1 % on 3DLoMatch with 5,000 correspondences, against 92.0 % and 75.0 % for GeoTransformer (Table 1).
On KITTI, 99.8 % registration recall with a relative translation error of 6.7 cm, the lowest in the comparison (Table 2).
Removing the topological structure encoding lowers recall to 89.7 % and 67.4 % on 3DMatch and 3DLoMatch (Table 3).

The indoor experiments use 3DMatch and its low-overlap split 3DLoMatch, which holds the scan pairs with 10–30 % overlap. Registration recall is the share of pairs whose estimated transformation has an RMSE below 0.2 m, computed with 50K RANSAC iterations. TopFormer’s registration recall is the highest, or tied for highest, at every correspondence number tested (5,000 down to 250) on both splits, and its feature matching recall on 3DMatch stays between 98.4 % and 98.7 %. Its inlier ratio is below GeoTransformer’s at 5,000 correspondences (71.7 % against 71.9 % on 3DMatch, 37.2 % against 43.5 % on 3DLoMatch), but higher at smaller numbers, for example 82.8 % against 76.0 % on 3DMatch and 53.1 % against 46.2 % on 3DLoMatch at 1,000. On the outdoor KITTI odometry data, most of the compared methods already reach 99.8 % recall; TopFormer matches that, with a rotation error of 0.27°.

The ablation study shows that both parts of the encoding contribute. Without the geodesic distance, registration recall falls from 92.4 % to 90.3 % on 3DMatch and from 75.1 % to 72.3 % on 3DLoMatch; without the normal-based directional terms it falls to 91.9 % and 73.9 %. Dropping the encoding entirely, which leaves a vanilla Transformer, costs 2.7 and 7.7 points of recall, and the inlier ratio falls by 8.6 and 5.6 points.

item.title: 3D Autoscan System
item.description:
A scanner + rotary platform pipeline that captures arbitrary objects to ~0.1 mm in under five minutes — built to seed a 3D shape database without per-object parameter tuning.

Figure 1. Scanner + rotary platform setup. Controlled by a single PC running the registration pipeline.

Problem

Building a 3D shape database requires scanning many objects. Off-the-shelf scanning is fine for one model, but at database scale it costs human hours: every object shape requires re-tuning algorithm parameters, and every mis-registration eats into the ~5 min/object budget. The need is a robust pipeline that adapts — per-object parameter tuning has to disappear.

Pipeline

The system fuses three algorithmic stages tuned to handle scale, reflectance, and pose variation without manual intervention.

Figure 2. Frame-to-frame point cloud + texture registration.

Figure 3. Environmental outlier removal.

Figure 4. Multi-pose global registration.

Frame-to-frame registration aligns sequential scans on both geometry and texture; an outlier removal stage strips away background noise; finally a global registration pass aligns the multiple platform poses into a coherent model.
